content.title: COOKING MISTAKES THAT QUIETLY {{DESTROY}} YOUR HEALTHY MEAL
facts: **Boiling vegetables** – Broccoli and spinach lose most of their vitamin C and B vitamins into the water; steam for 4-5 minutes instead to keep nutrients in the food, not the sink.
**Olive oil at high heat** – Extra virgin olive oil breaks down and smokes above roughly 190°C, turning heart-healthy fats into harmful compounds; save it for dressings or low-medium heat cooking.
**Adding salt too early** – Salting beans or lentils at the start of cooking makes them stay tough for longer; add salt in the last 10 minutes for both flavor and texture.
**Microwaving in plastic containers** – Heat can cause chemicals from plastic to leach into food, even in 'microwave-safe' containers; switch to glass or ceramic before reheating.
**Overcooking eggs** – Rubbery, grey-edged yolks form when eggs are cooked too long or too hot, breaking down some of their protein quality; cook low and slow instead.
**Draining canned beans without rinsing** – The liquid is loaded with added sodium; a quick rinse under water cuts the sodium content significantly.
**Cutting vegetables long before cooking** – Pre-chopped veggies lose vitamin C the longer they sit exposed to air; chop right before you cook or eat them.
**Reusing the same cutting board** – Switching straight from raw chicken to salad greens without washing the board is one of the most common ways foodborne bacteria spread at home.

caption:
A few of these mistakes are easier to fix than you'd think. Take boiling vegetables: when you dump broccoli into a pot of water, water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C and folate actually dissolve OUT of the vegetable and into the liquid you're about to pour down the drain — steaming keeps those nutrients trapped inside the food itself. Then there's olive oil: heating it past its smoke point doesn't just ruin the taste, it triggers oxidation that creates compounds linked to inflammation, which cancels out the whole reason you chose olive oil in the first place. And with eggs, overcooking denatures the proteins so aggressively that your body actually absorbs less of the protein compared to a soft, gently cooked egg. Everyone's kitchen habits are different, so start with whichever one feels easiest to change first.
